faq.a: Neurons in the cauda equina are vulnerable to ischemia; decompression within 48 h markedly improves motor and sphincter recovery.
faq.q: Why is time to surgery so critical?

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden low back pain, bilateral foot drop and inability to void. What is your immediate next step — arrange urgent MRI and call the spine team for decompression within 48 h.
During examination you find absent anal wink but normal lower‑extremity reflexes. Which diagnosis does this most support — cauda equina syndrome rather than conus medullaris.

A patient with known HIV develops back pain and fever. MRI shows a posterior epidural collection. Which management principle is essential — start broad‑spectrum antibiotics and plan urgent surgical drainage, while avoiding steroids until infection is ruled out.
You have only a CT scanner available. How do you proceed to confirm compression — perform CT myelogram with contrast to delineate the thecal sac and guide surgery.

Post‑operative day 2, the patient still cannot void despite catheter removal. What does this indicate — ongoing sacral nerve injury; continue bladder training and consider repeat imaging if no improvement.

Which feature distinguishes conus medullaris syndrome from cauda equina syndrome — early bowel dysfunction with upper motor neuron signs in conus, whereas CES shows saddle anaesthesia and LMN leg weakness.
A young adult with a large central disc herniation refuses surgery. What is the risk of non‑operative management — permanent sphincter loss and irreversible motor deficit.
In a low‑resource hospital, a patient cannot get MRI. What alternative investigation can you use — bedside bladder scan and CT myelogram to assess retention and level of compression.
ai.title: Cauda Equina Syndrome
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Cauda equina syndrome is an emergency compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and lower‑motor‑neuron leg weakness. Prompt recognition, imaging and decompression are essential to prevent permanent disability.

b: Saddle anaesthesia (loss of sensation in perineum, inner thighs, genitalia)
Areflexic bladder (urinary retention or overflow incontinence)
Loss of anal tone or perianal sensation
Bilateral lower‑motor‑neuron leg weakness, especially foot dorsiflexion
sections.p: A syndrome of acute or sub‑acute compression of the cauda equina nerve roots below L2, producing a characteristic clinical picture. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by imaging.

b: Stage I: mild sensory loss, no bladder dysfunction
Stage II: saddle anaesthesia with urinary retention, motor strength ≥3/5
Stage III: severe motor weakness <3/5, bowel incontinence
sections.p: Severity is graded by neurological deficit and timing of decompression. Early (<48 h) surgery yields better functional recovery.

b: Large central lumbar disc herniation (L4‑L5, L5‑S1)
Spinal metastases (breast, prostate, lung)
Epidural abscess (often Staphylococcus aureus, TB, HIV‑related)
Traumatic fracture‑dislocation of the lumbar spine
Post‑operative hematoma or iatrogenic stenosis
sections.p: Most cases are due to mechanical compression; in low‑resource settings infectious and inflammatory causes are also common.

b: Severe low back pain, often worsening on standing
Bilateral leg weakness, especially foot drop
Saddle anaesthesia, perineal numbness
Urinary retention or overflow incontinence
Loss of anal wink or reduced perianal sensation
sections.p: Patients usually present with acute low back pain radiating to the legs, followed by sensory and autonomic changes.
Imaging confirms the level and cause of compression; bedside tests assess autonomic function when imaging is delayed.

t.b: What is the cause and level of compression? – Shows disc material, tumour, abscess or hematoma; guides surgical planning
What is the compressive lesion? – Provides detailed bony anatomy and contrast‑filled CSF space; useful where MRI is not accessible

t.a: Perianal sensation test and anal tone (digital rectal exam)
t.b: Is sacral nerve function impaired? – Absent sensation or tone supports CES
Is infection likely? – Elevated WCC/CRP suggests epidural abscess; normal values do not exclude it

b: Progressive motor weakness within hours
Increasing urinary retention despite catheterisation
Bowel incontinence
Severe, unrelenting back pain not relieved by analgesia
sections.p: Delay in diagnosis leads to irreversible neurologic loss and chronic disability.

b: Emergency laminectomy and disc/abscess removal within 48 h
High‑dose intravenous antibiotics for epidural abscess (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) – avoid aminoglycosides due to nephrotoxicity
Antitubercular therapy if TB abscess suspected – start before surgery if diagnosis clear
Steroids are not routinely recommended; may be used briefly for severe edema if no infection
Bladder catheterisation and bowel regimen to prevent retention complications
sections.p: Urgent surgical decompression plus targeted medical therapy for the underlying cause.

b: Daily neurologic exam for first week
Physiotherapy for gait and strength
Educate on avoiding heavy lifting and early treatment of disc disease
Screen for HIV, TB or chronic infections in recurrent cases
sections.p: Post‑operative monitoring of neurologic recovery and rehabilitation are essential.

b: Spinal stenosis – chronic, progressive, usually no acute bladder loss
Conus medullaris syndrome – upper motor neuron signs, early bowel dysfunction, lesion above L1
Peripheral neuropathy – distal sensory loss, no saddle anaesthesia
sections.p: Conditions that cause back pain and neurologic deficits but differ in management.

CT may miss small soft‑tissue disc fragments that MRI would show
